messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  (none)

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  (none)

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Raj, a 34-year-old South Asian male and a delivery driver, has been struggling with intense guilt and self-blame since a traumatic incident he experienced at work several months ago. On that fateful day, Raj was delivering packages in the dense traffic of downtown Los Angeles when another vehicle abruptly swerved into his lane. Despite his best efforts to avoid the collision, his truck struck the other car, causing severe injuries to its driver. The trauma of the event has left Raj with a profound sense of failure and an unrelenting burden of guilt. Since the accident, Raj has been plagued by thoughts that he should have done more to prevent the crash. He often replays the incident in his mind, analyzing every split-second decision he made on that day. The weight of these negative appraisals has become so heavy that he frequently questions whether he can continue driving without causing another accident. His belief that "I should have protected others and I failed" is a recurring theme in his internal dialogue. Raj’s self-blame extends beyond the immediate event to encompass broader aspects of his life. He often feels that the accident was a direct result of his actions, leading him to question not only his driving skills but also his judgment as an overall person. His conviction that "The event happened because of the way I acted" has seeped into other areas of his life, causing him significant distress and affecting his daily functioning. In his marriage, Raj’s preoccupation with guilt and self-blame has strained his relationship with his wife. He often feels unworthy of her love and support, which leads to periods where he withdraws emotionally. This withdrawal is not intentional; rather, it stems from his deep-seated belief that he deserves punishment for the accident. His wife has noticed a change in him but struggles to understand why he seems so distant. The guilt has also affected Raj’s performance at work. He now drives with an excessive level of caution, constantly second-guessing every decision on the road. This heightened state of alertness often leaves him exhausted and anxious by the end of each shift. His colleagues have commented on his more cautious behavior but are unaware of the emotional turmoil he is experiencing. Raj’s thoughts about inaction guilt—"I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened"—have taken a toll on his mental health. He has started to isolate himself from social activities and no longer enjoys spending time with friends or family. The thought of facing others, knowing that he could have prevented the accident, is too overwhelming. What finally brought Raj to seek help was an incident at home where his wife expressed her concern about his emotional state. She noticed that he had been increasingly withdrawn and stressed out, and she encouraged him to talk to someone who could provide support. Despite his reluctance, Raj realized that he needed help to cope with the guilt and self-blame. In therapy, Raj is most afraid of being judged or not being able to forgive himself for what happened. He hopes to find a way to move past these feelings of failure and reconnect with his family and work life. His primary goal is to regain a sense of peace and acceptance, which he believes will help him overcome the lingering trauma from that fateful day on the road.
